stops.name: Jerusalem, the oath, the water, the ring of Solomon
stops.campa: In the Glory of Kings, Solomon, captivated by Makeda, bids her stay the night; she consents on one oath: that he take nothing of hers by force. He binds her by the like oath. At the feast he serves food seasoned to burning thirst, and in the night she rises for the water set by the bed and drinks. He wakes: the water is mine, he says, and you are released from your oath as I from mine. Thus is Menelik conceived. At her leaving he gives her a ring for a token, that if she bear a son he may know his father by it.
stops.quote: Verily thou hast broken thine oath that thou wouldst not take anything by force that is in my house.
stops.quote_source: Kebra Nagast, ch. 30 (the oath and the water)

stops.name: Aksum, Menelik returns; the Ark comes to Zion in Ethiopia
stops.campa: The son grows in his mother's land; coming of age he asks who his father is, and Makeda gives him the ring and sends him up to Jerusalem. Solomon knows him at once by his face, the image of David, and by the token; he anoints him king of Ethiopia as Menelik. But the firstborn of the priests, sent to attend him home, carry away the Ark of the Covenant, the Tabot, Zion, some say with heaven's leave, borne bloodless from the sanctuary. It comes to Aksum, and Makeda receives it, and sets it in the house that becomes the Church of Mary of Zion.
stops.quote: How is it that ye have come without letting me know, whereas when ye came before ye showed me honour?
stops.quote_source: Kebra Nagast, ch. 53 (the coming of Zion to Ethiopia)

stops.name: The House of the Forest of Lebanon, the shields of beaten gold
stops.campa: Thirteen years Solomon builds his own house, and the House of the Forest of Lebanon: a hundred cubits long, upon four rows of cedar pillars, so that it seems a forest brought indoors. There he sets two hundred targets and three hundred shields of beaten gold, six hundred shekels of gold to a target. All his drinking vessels are gold; none is of silver, for silver is counted as nothing in the days of Solomon. He makes silver in Jerusalem to be as stones, and cedars as the sycamore trees of the vale for abundance. The throne of the lions stands within, and the king's cup is never empty.
stops.quote: And king Solomon made two hundred targets of beaten gold: six hundred shekels of gold went to one target.

stops.name: Megiddo, the chariot-cities, the store-cities, Hazor and Gezer
stops.campa: This is the reason of the levy Solomon raises: to build the house of the Lord, and his own house, and the Millo, and the wall of Jerusalem, and Hazor, and Megiddo, and Gezer. He fortifies the great cities of the plain and the passes, the store-cities and the cities for his chariots and horsemen; and Beth-horon the nether, and Baalath, and all the cities of his desire. The peoples that remain, Amorite, Hittite, Perizzite, Hivite, Jebusite, he levies for the toil, but of Israel he makes no bondmen. At Megiddo and Hazor and Gezer the same great six-chambered gates rise, cut to one measure.
stops.quote: And this is the reason of the levy which king Solomon raised; for to build the house of the LORD, and his own house, and Millo, and the wall of Jerusalem, and Hazor, and Megiddo, and Gezer.

stops.name: Tadmor in the wilderness, the city on the desert road
stops.campa: Beyond the settled land Solomon builds Tadmor in the wilderness: the oasis of palms on the caravan road between the sown country and the Euphrates, where the springs rise in the desert. He girdles his dominion with cities from the Red Sea shore to the edge of the eastern waste, holding the trade of the world along his roads: the spice from the south, the gold from Ophir, the horses out of Egypt and Kue his merchants buy by droves. The wisest king lays out a city where there is only sand and water, and the desert route runs safe under his hand from Egypt unto the great River.
stops.quote: And Tadmor in the wilderness, in the land.

stops.name: Ezion-geber, the navy of Tarshish, the apes and peacocks
stops.campa: At Ezion-geber, beside Eloth on the shore of the Red Sea in the land of Edom, Solomon makes a navy of ships, and Hiram sends his shipmen that have knowledge of the sea to sail with the servants of Solomon. They go to Ophir and fetch from thence gold, four hundred and twenty talents, and bring it to the king. Once in three years the navy of Tarshish comes home, bringing gold and silver, ivory, and apes, and peacocks. So King Solomon exceeds all the kings of the earth for riches and for wisdom; all the earth seeks his presence, to hear the wisdom God has put in his heart.
stops.quote: For the king had at sea a navy of Tharshish with the navy of Hiram: once in three years came the navy of Tharshish, bringing gold, and silver, ivory, and apes, and peacocks.

stops.name: The Mount of Olives, the high places for strange gods
stops.campa: King Solomon loves many strange women: seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines; and when he is old his wives turn away his heart after other gods. He goes after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites. On the hill before Jerusalem, on the Mount of Olives, he builds a high place for Chemosh the abomination of Moab, and for Molech the abomination of Ammon, and so for all his strange wives, who burn incense to their gods. The Lord is angry with Solomon, because his heart is turned from the God of Israel, which had appeared to him twice.
stops.quote: For it came to pass, when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods: and his heart was not perfect with the LORD his God.

stops.name: The field outside Jerusalem, Ahijah rends the garment for Jeroboam
stops.campa: Because Solomon's heart is turned, the Lord raises up adversaries against him: Hadad the Edomite, Rezon of Damascus, and Jeroboam the son of Nebat, set over the levy of the house of Joseph. As Jeroboam goes out of Jerusalem, the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite meets him alone in the field, clad in a new garment; and Ahijah rends it into twelve pieces. Take ten pieces, he says, for thus saith the Lord: I will rend the kingdom from the hand of Solomon and give ten tribes to you, but one tribe shall remain to David's line, for Jerusalem's sake. The tearing is spoken before the king is cold.
stops.quote: Behold, I will rend the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon, and will give ten tribes to thee.

stops.name: The exile of Koheleth, the ring lost to Asmodeus
stops.campa: In the aggadah the demon Asmodeus, freed of his chains, tricks Solomon into loosing the ring with the Name and swallows it, then hurls the king four hundred leagues away and sits upon the throne in Solomon's very shape. The true king wanders the roads as a beggar, from city to city, crying in every place: 'I, Koheleth, was king over Israel in Jerusalem.' None believe him. At length the ring, cast into the sea, is swallowed by a fish set before Solomon; he cuts it open and finds the Name, and the counterfeit flees shrieking. The king recovers his throne, humbled, knowing the vanity of glory.
stops.quote: I the Preacher was king over Israel in Jerusalem.
stops.quote_source: Ecclesiastes 1:12 (the cry of the aggadah; Talmud Gittin 68b)

stops.name: Jerusalem, Koheleth's word: vanity of vanities
stops.campa: Restored and old, the king who has had all things, houses, vineyards, pools, servants, silver and gold, singers, and every delight of the sons of men, sets down the summing of his days. He has seen all the works done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and vexation of spirit. Wisdom he found, and much grief with it; there is a time for everything under heaven, and one event happens to the wise and to the fool alike. He gives the conclusion: fear God, and keep His commandments, for this is the whole of man. The wisest of kings names the emptiness of his kingdom.
stops.quote: Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.

stops.name: The Temple, the death upon the staff and the worm
stops.campa: When God decrees the death of Sulayman, he is standing in the sanctuary, leaning upon his staff, overseeing the jinn still bound to the last of the work. His soul is taken, and yet he does not fall; he stands as if in prayer, and the demons labour on, not knowing, believing the king watches. Only the creature of the earth, the little worm, gnaws slowly through the wood of the staff, day upon day, until it is eaten away, and the king falls. Then the jinn perceive that he is dead, and know that had they known the unseen, they would not have stayed in the humiliating toil.
stops.quote: Then, when We decreed (Solomon's) death, nothing showed them his death except a little worm of the earth, which kept (slowly) gnawing away at his staff: so when he fell down, the Jinns saw plainly that if they had known the unseen, they would not have tarried in the humiliating Penalty (of their Task).
